Literal Interpretation

The Birth of Isaac

Genesis 21 opens with the long-awaited fulfillment of God's promise to Abraham and Sarah. "And the Lord visited Sarah, as he had promised: and fulfilled what he had spoken. And she conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time that God had foretold her" (Gen 21:1-2). After twenty-five years of waiting, the patriarch and his wife, both advanced in years far beyond the natural capacity for childbearing, receive the son of promise.

St. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on Genesis, emphasizes the divine intervention that made this birth possible:

"After first foretelling the birth of Isaac, He then accomplished it; comparing this to how Christians' birth in Christ was also announced before by all the Prophets and then brought to pass."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis

The birth of Isaac demonstrates that nothing is impossible with God. Abraham was one hundred years old (Gen 21:5), and Sarah was ninety, yet God's word proved faithful. The text emphasizes Abraham's obedience: "And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac the eighth day, as God had commanded him" (Gen 21:4). This immediate compliance with the divine command regarding circumcision shows the patriarch's unwavering fidelity to the covenant.

Sarah's Laughter Transformed

The name Isaac (Yitschaq) means "he laughs" or "laughter." This name commemorates both Abraham's laughter of wonder when the promise was first given (Gen 17:17) and Sarah's laughter of incredulity when she overheard the angelic visitors (Gen 18:12). Now Sarah declares: "God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears will laugh with me" (Gen 21:6).

St. Augustine, in his interpretation of this passage, distinguishes between the different kinds of laughter:

"Some wonder why the Lord only rebuked Sarah, while Abraham also laughed. The reason is that Abraham's laughter was one of admiration and joy. Sarah's, however, was originated by doubt, and God, who knows the hearts of men, could distinguish one laugh from another."

St. Augustine, Questions on Genesis

What began as doubt has been transformed into joy. Sarah's laughter of disbelief has become laughter of wonder and gratitude. The very name of her son will forever remind Israel that God keeps His promises, however impossible they may seem to human reason.

The Weaning Feast and Ishmael's Mocking

The child grew and was weaned, and Abraham made a great feast on the day of Isaac's weaning (Gen 21:8). Weaning in the ancient Near East typically occurred between ages two and five, marking a significant milestone in the child's development and survival. At this celebration, however, conflict erupts: "And when Sara had seen the son of Agar the Egyptian playing with Isaac her son, she said to Abraham: Cast out this bondwoman, and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with my son Isaac" (Gen 21:9-10).

St. John Chrysostom, in his 46th Homily on Genesis, provides a nuanced reading of Ishmael's conduct:

"John does not offer a particularly nefarious interpretation of Ishmael's play with Isaac. Yet the consequences were significant, for Ishmael's behavior raised concerns about the inheritance and the security of the promised line."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis, Homily 46

The Hebrew word metsacheq ("playing" or "laughing") is ambiguous and may suggest mockery or scorn. The Apostle Paul later interprets this as persecution: "But as then he, that was born according to the flesh, persecuted him that was after the spirit; so also it is now" (Gal 4:29).

The Expulsion of Hagar and Ishmael

Sarah's demand troubled Abraham greatly because he loved Ishmael, his firstborn son. Yet God instructs Abraham to comply: "Let it not seem grievous to thee for the boy, and for thy bondwoman: in all that Sara hath said to thee, hearken to her voice: for in Isaac shall thy seed be called" (Gen 21:12). God also promises that Ishmael will become a great nation because he is Abraham's offspring (Gen 21:13).

Chrysostom validates Abraham's decision while noting God's care for the expelled:

"The patriarch followed his wife's wishes completely because he said '[Hagar] is not a concern of mine; one thing alone concerns me, to keep [Sarah] undisturbed, without distress, free from any sorrow and enjoying the highest respect.' Though John thus validates Abraham and Sarah's expulsion of Hagar, he underlines the fact that Hagar received 'favour from on high' as she was comforted and guided by an angel of the Lord."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis

Abraham rises early, gives Hagar bread and a skin of water, and sends her away with Ishmael. When the water is exhausted in the wilderness of Beersheba, Hagar places the child under a shrub and sits at a distance, unable to watch him die. But God hears the boy's voice, and the angel of God calls to Hagar, promising that Ishmael will become a great nation. God opens her eyes to see a well of water, and they survive (Gen 21:14-21).

The Covenant at Beersheba

The chapter concludes with the covenant between Abraham and Abimelech, king of Gerar (Gen 21:22-34). Abimelech, recognizing that God is with Abraham in all he does, seeks a treaty of mutual non-aggression. Abraham agrees but also raises a complaint about a well that Abimelech's servants had seized. The two men make a covenant, and Abraham sets apart seven ewe lambs as witness to his ownership of the well.

The name Beersheba (Be'er Sheva) has a dual meaning: "Well of the Oath" and "Well of Seven," commemorating both the covenant oath and the seven lambs. As one commentary notes:

"'Beersheba' means 'well of the oath' and can also be interpreted as 'well of seven,' a reference to the seven gift lambs. The Hebrew words for 'seven' and 'oath' come from the same root word: 'Seba.'"

Traditional commentary

Abraham plants a tamarisk tree and calls upon the name of the Lord, the everlasting God (El Olam). This divine title emphasizes God's eternal faithfulness to His covenant promises. The patriarch then dwells in the land of the Philistines for many days, establishing a permanent presence in the promised land.
allegorical:
Allegorical Interpretation

Isaac as Type of Christ

The birth of Isaac after long barrenness and in apparent impossibility is a figure of the birth of Christ. As Isaac was born contrary to the natural order through divine intervention, so Christ was born of a virgin by the power of the Holy Spirit. St. Clement of Alexandria draws out this typological connection:

"He is Isaac, who is a type of the Lord, a child as a son; for he was the son of Abraham, as Christ the Son of God, and a sacrifice as the Lord, but he was not immolated as the Lord. Isaac only bore the wood of the sacrifice, as the Lord the wood of the cross."

St. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus

Furthermore, Clement notes the mystical significance of Isaac's name: "Isaac laughed mystically, prophesying that the Lord should fill us with joy." The laughter that gives Isaac his name anticipates the joy that Christ brings to the world through His incarnation and redemption.

Sarah and Hagar: The Two Covenants

The Apostle Paul provides the authoritative allegorical interpretation of this chapter in his Epistle to the Galatians: "For it is written that Abraham had two sons: the one by a bondwoman, and the other by a free woman... Which things are an allegory. For these are the two testaments" (Gal 4:22-24). The Church Fathers developed this Pauline allegory extensively.

St. Augustine, in his City of God, explains the typology:

"Citizens are begotten to the earthly city by nature vitiated by sin, but to the heavenly city by grace freeing nature from sin; whence the former are called 'vessels of wrath,' the latter 'vessels of mercy.' This was typified in the two sons of Abraham: Ishmael, the son of Hagar the handmaid, being born according to the flesh, while Isaac was born of the free woman Sarah, according to the promise. In one birth, human action is revealed; in the other, divine kindness comes to light."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XV

Sarah represents the New Covenant of grace, the heavenly Jerusalem, the Church of Christ. Hagar represents the Old Covenant of the Law, the earthly Jerusalem, bondage to sin. Augustine further explains:

"Sarah, the free woman, who prefigured the free city (which again was also prefigured in another way by that shadow of a city Jerusalem), therefore said, 'Cast out the bond woman and her son; for the son of the bond woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.'"

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XV

Isaac and Ishmael: Spirit and Flesh

Origen, in his Homilies on Genesis, elaborates on the opposition between the two sons:

"Those who live 'according to the flesh' are children of Hagar and thereby stand opposed to those who live 'according to the spirit,' that is to say, believers in Christ who are real heirs to the Abrahamic promise. Ishmael and Isaac represent the flesh and the spirit respectively."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis

Ishmael was born according to the natural order, representing what human effort can achieve apart from divine grace. Isaac was born according to the promise, representing the supernatural life that comes only through faith in God's word. The conflict between them prefigures the perpetual struggle between the flesh and the spirit in the life of every believer.

Medieval interpreters developed this further:

"Abraham is understood as God the Father, Hagar as the old law, Ishmael as the carnal people, Sarah as the new law, Isaac as the Christian people. The Church, established under grace, with the Christian people is enriched with the kingdom of God."

Medieval patristic interpretation

The Heavenly Jerusalem

Sarah's freedom corresponds to the heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of all believers. As Paul writes: "But the Jerusalem which is above is free: which is our mother" (Gal 4:26). The Church, born from above through baptism, is the true seed of Abraham, heirs of the promise through faith in Christ.

"The heavenly Jerusalem 'produces not slave children, but free children.' These are children who are not under the law as a means of justification, but children who rest in the finished work of Jesus Christ."

Traditional patristic interpretation

The Circumcision on the Eighth Day

Abraham circumcised Isaac on the eighth day as God commanded (Gen 21:4). The eighth day carries profound typological significance. St. Augustine, in his disputation with Faustus, explains:

"Christ brought it about that His body rested from all its works on Sabbath in the tomb, and that His resurrection on the third day, which we call the Lord's day, the day after the Sabbath, and therefore the eighth, proved the circumcision of the eighth day to be also prophetical of Him. For Augustine, circumcision meant the eradication of the mortality which comes from our carnal generation."

St. Augustine, Contra Faustum

The eighth day is the day of resurrection, the day of the new creation. As the Venerable Bede teaches:

"Circumcision under the law wrought the same healing against the wound of original sin as does baptism in this time of revealed grace... The time of this most longed-for entrance is that eighth day on which the circumcision is celebrated."

Venerable Bede, Homily on the Circumcision

The Well of Beersheba

Origen saw profound spiritual significance in the wells dug by the patriarchs. In his homilies, he interprets the wells as sources of divine wisdom and spiritual truth:

"If I shall wish to dig deeply and open the hidden veins of living water, immediately the Philistines will be present and will strive with me. They will stir up disputes and malicious charges against me and will begin to refill my wells with their earth and mud."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis

The well at Beersheba, over which Abraham made a covenant, prefigures the living water that Christ offers. The "Well of the Oath" points to the baptismal waters sealed by God's covenant promise, while the "Well of Seven" suggests the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit.

The Tamarisk Tree

Abraham plants a tamarisk tree at Beersheba (Gen 21:33). This tree, which provides shade and sustenance in the desert, is seen by the Fathers as a figure of the Cross, under whose shadow the faithful find refuge and life. Just as travelers found rest beneath Abraham's tree, so all who come to Christ crucified find rest for their souls.
moral:
Moral (Tropological) Interpretation

The Virtue of Patience

Abraham and Sarah waited twenty-five years for the fulfillment of God's promise. This extended period of patient waiting offers profound moral instruction for the Christian life. Abraham was seventy-five when God first called him (Gen 12:4) and one hundred when Isaac was born (Gen 21:5). Throughout this quarter century, he had to maintain faith in the face of apparent impossibility.

"Abraham was blessed with the patience to take a long-term view. God's promises were to be realized in the time of Abraham's offspring, not in the time of Abraham himself. Abraham ended up patiently waiting for the timing of the Lord for a quarter of a century! These 25 years were just to see the beginning of that promise being fulfilled."

Traditional moral interpretation

This patience was not passive resignation but active trust: "As Hebrews 6:15 says, Abraham had to wait patiently. But Abraham did not just do nothing. Instead, he had faith (active belief and trust in God)." The moral lesson is clear: God's timing is not our timing, and the virtue of patience enables us to persevere in hope even when fulfillment seems impossibly distant.

Obedience Even When Understanding Fails

God's command to send away Hagar and Ishmael was deeply painful to Abraham: "Abraham was very much grieved on account of his son" (Gen 21:11, Vulgate rendering). Yet when God confirmed that he should listen to Sarah's voice, Abraham obeyed immediately, rising early the next morning to carry out the difficult task (Gen 21:14).

"Those who fear the Lord come to know him in such a way that they'll do whatever he asks because they deeply trust him and believe that he's good. Fearing the Lord means trusting the Lord means obeying the Lord. Abraham's obedience showed that he trusted God, even when he did not feel like it."

Traditional moral commentary

This teaches us that obedience to God must sometimes override our natural affections and our limited understanding. Abraham could not see how God would care for Ishmael in the wilderness, but he trusted that God's command was wise and good. True faith obeys even when it cannot comprehend.

The Danger of Compromise

The presence of Ishmael in Abraham's household was the fruit of an earlier compromise. When Sarah proposed that Abraham take Hagar as a concubine (Gen 16:2), Abraham agreed rather than waiting for God's promised son through Sarah. This impatience led to decades of domestic strife and the painful necessity of sending Ishmael away.

"Ishmael was born according to the flesh, born of human effort and impatience, while Isaac was the son of the promise, born of faith and obedience."

Traditional moral interpretation

The moral application is sobering: our attempts to "help" God fulfill His promises through worldly means often create complications that we and our descendants must painfully resolve. Better to wait in patient faith than to grasp at premature solutions through fleshly wisdom.

Casting Out the Works of the Flesh

The expulsion of Hagar and Ishmael has direct application to the spiritual life. Origen draws out the moral lesson:

"God told Abraham to expel Ishmael (the child of the flesh) because God's covenant promise was through Isaac alone (the child of the Spirit). From this, God reveals that your spiritual renewal requires that you make no accommodation with your flesh."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis

Just as there could be no coexistence between Ishmael and Isaac in Abraham's household, so there can be no compromise between the flesh and the spirit in the Christian soul. The works of the flesh must be cast out so that the fruits of the Spirit may flourish. This is not a one-time event but an ongoing discipline of mortification and growth in grace.

God's Providence in the Wilderness

The account of Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness demonstrates God's providential care even for those outside the primary line of promise. When Hagar despaired of life, God heard Ishmael's voice and sent an angel with words of comfort. God opened Hagar's eyes to see the well that would save them (Gen 21:17-19).

"She began to use a new name for God. She said to him, 'You are God Who Sees Me.' She said this because she thought, 'I see that even in this place God sees me and cares for me!'"

Traditional interpretation

The moral lesson is that God's mercy extends beyond what we might expect. Even in our wilderness experiences, when we feel cast out and abandoned, God sees us and provides. No one is beyond the reach of His providential care.

Keeping Covenants and Speaking Truth

The covenant between Abraham and Abimelech teaches the importance of honesty and faithfulness in human relationships. Abraham dealt truthfully with Abimelech regarding the well, raising his legitimate complaint rather than nursing resentment. The two men resolved their dispute through open communication and sealed their agreement with a covenant.

Abraham's conduct at Beersheba demonstrates that the people of God should be known for their integrity in all dealings. The Christian's word should be trustworthy, contracts should be honored, and disputes should be resolved honestly rather than through deception or force.

Worship and Gratitude

After establishing the covenant with Abimelech, Abraham planted a tamarisk tree and "called upon the name of the Lord, the everlasting God" (Gen 21:33). This act of worship in the midst of daily life shows that the faithful soul recognizes God's hand in temporal blessings and responds with prayer and thanksgiving.

The title El Olam ("the everlasting God") expresses Abraham's growing understanding of the divine nature. God is not merely a local deity of this place or that, but the eternal Lord of all times and places. This theological insight should shape our own worship, lifting our hearts from passing concerns to the unchanging faithfulness of the eternal God.

Joy in Fulfillment

Sarah's transformed laughter reminds us that faith, though tested through long waiting, ends in joy. "God has made me laugh" she declares (Gen 21:6). The Christian life, though marked by trials and patient endurance, is oriented toward the joy of fulfillment. As the Psalmist writes: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy" (Ps 125:5).
anagogical:
Anagogical Interpretation

Isaac's Birth and the Resurrection

The birth of Isaac to aged parents who were "as good as dead" (Heb 11:12) prefigures the resurrection of the body. What was humanly impossible became reality through divine power. So too, the resurrection of the dead, impossible by natural means, will be accomplished by the same God who brought life from Sarah's barren womb.

St. Clement of Alexandria perceived in Isaac a type of the risen Christ:

"An intimation of the divinity of the Lord in His not having been slain. For Jesus rose again after his burial, having suffered no harm, like Isaac released from sacrifice."

St. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus

Isaac's deliverance from death on Mount Moriah (Genesis 22) is foreshadowed here in his miraculous birth, for both events point to the resurrection victory of Christ. The laughter of Isaac anticipates the eternal joy of the risen saints.

The Eighth Day and Eternal Life

The circumcision of Isaac on the eighth day (Gen 21:4) carries profound eschatological significance. The Church Fathers understood the eighth day as the symbol of eternity, the day beyond the seven-day week of earthly time. St. Thomas Aquinas taught:

"The figurative reason for the choice of the day points to the following mystery: that in the eighth period of time, the time of the resurrection, on the eighth day, spiritual circumcision will be accomplished by Christ."

St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae

In the resurrection, believers will receive their glorified bodies, perfected and freed from all corruption. This is the "spiritual circumcision" of which the eighth day is a sign, the final cutting away of all that belongs to the old nature and the flesh.

The Venerable Bede makes explicit the connection between circumcision and heavenly glory:

"We will enter the forecourt of the heavenly kingdom to behold forever the face of the Creator. This is prefigured by the circumcision of the little ones in the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem... The time of this most longed-for entrance is that eighth day on which the circumcision is celebrated."

Venerable Bede, Homily on the Circumcision

The Heavenly Jerusalem

Sarah, the free woman, is a type of the heavenly Jerusalem, the eternal city whose citizens are the redeemed. St. Augustine develops this imagery extensively:

"Fitly, therefore, does Isaac, the child of promise, typify the children of grace, the citizens of the free city."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XV

The children of Sarah are destined for the city described in the Apocalypse: "And I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband" (Rev 21:2). This heavenly Jerusalem, of which the earthly Jerusalem was only a shadow, is the final home of all who are born according to the Spirit.

"The heavenly Jerusalem, the true church from above, represented by Sarah, is in a state of freedom, and is the mother of all believers, who are born of the Holy Spirit."

Traditional patristic interpretation

The Inheritance of the Saints

Sarah's insistence that Ishmael "shall not be heir with my son Isaac" (Gen 21:10) has eschatological implications. The inheritance of the saints is not a temporal kingdom but eternal glory. Those born according to the flesh cannot inherit the kingdom of God; only those born of the Spirit will share in the heavenly inheritance.

As St. Paul teaches: "Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God: neither shall corruption inherit incorruption" (1 Cor 15:50). The expulsion of Ishmael prefigures the final separation of the wheat from the chaff, when those who have lived according to the flesh will be excluded from the kingdom, while those who have lived according to the Spirit will inherit eternal life.

The Well of Living Water

The well at Beersheba, which sustained Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness and over which Abraham made his covenant, points forward to the eternal springs of paradise. Origen interpreted the patriarchal wells as sources of divine wisdom:

"Observe each detail which has been written. For, if one knows how to dig into the depth, he will find a treasure in the details, and perhaps also, the precious jewels of the mysteries lie hidden where they are not esteemed."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis

In the heavenly city, the faithful will drink from the river of the water of life: "And he showed me a river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb" (Rev 22:1). The wells that sustained the patriarchs in the desert were types of this eternal fountain, glimpses of the unending refreshment that awaits the saints.

The Everlasting God

Abraham invoked God as El Olam, "the everlasting God" (Gen 21:33). This divine title expresses God's eternity, His existence beyond all time and change. The anagogical significance is that believers are called to share in this eternity. As St. Augustine taught, the restless human heart finds its rest only in the eternal God.

The eternity of God is the ground of our hope for eternal life. Because He is El Olam, His promises endure forever. The covenant He made with Abraham extends through Isaac to all who believe, culminating in the everlasting covenant of the new Jerusalem, where "He that shall overcome shall possess these things, and I will be his God: and he shall be my son" (Rev 21:7).

Joy Everlasting

The transformation of Sarah's laughter from doubt to joy anticipates the eternal joy of the blessed. St. Clement wrote that "Isaac laughed mystically, prophesying that the Lord should fill us with joy." This joy, begun in the present life through faith, will be perfected in the beatific vision.

As our Lord promised: "Your sorrow shall be turned into joy... and your joy no man shall take from you" (Jn 16:20-22). The temporary sorrows of this life, the long waitings and apparent impossibilities, will give way to laughter that never ends. Isaac's name, "he laughs," is a prophecy of the everlasting joy of the kingdom of heaven, where all tears will be wiped away and the faithful will rejoice forever in the presence of God.

The Sabbath Rest

Abraham's dwelling at Beersheba, where he planted the tamarisk tree and called upon the everlasting God, represents the rest that awaits the people of God. The Letter to the Hebrews teaches: "There remaineth therefore a day of rest for the people of God" (Heb 4:9).

This heavenly Sabbath is not idleness but perfect activity, the full flourishing of the soul in the vision of God. As one theological summary expresses it:

"The Sabbath rest is typological of the future rest of all believers in the new heavens and new earth... in which the saints, happy in souls and body, will rest in God from the sins, calamities, and miseries of this life."

Traditional eschatological interpretation

The tamarisk tree that Abraham planted, providing shade in the desert heat, is a figure of the tree of life in paradise, whose leaves are "for the healing of the nations" (Rev 22:2). Under that tree, in the garden city of God, the faithful will find their eternal home, dwelling forever in the land that was promised to Abraham and to his seed.
